autor: Angelo Clareno (c. 1250–1337), Spiritual Franciscan, from 1317 a Celestine hermit, writing in Italy
quelle: Historia septem tribulationum ordinis minorum, sixth tribulation and the beginning of the seventh, ed. Franz Ehrle in 'Die Spiritualen, ihr Verhältniss zum Franciscanerorden und zu den Fraticellen', Archiv für Litteratur- und Kirchengeschichte des Mittelalters II (Berlin: Weidmann, 1886), pp. 125–155. Internet Archive, gri_33125006414433 (Getty Research Institute). Public domain.
hinweis: Ehrle printed this part of the Historia from a manuscript of the Biblioteca Laurenziana, with the variants of a second Latin manuscript and of an early Italian translation; his text is kept with its medieval spelling, without his folio marks and apparatus. The OCR of this printing is good, and each excerpt was read against the page images. A modern critical edition of the whole work exists and is in copyright; it is not used. Twelve excerpts; cuts are marked […]. The English is this site's working translation (CC0).

sections.blurb: The Spirituals' history of their order as a history of persecution, written in exile by Angelo Clareno, who was there: Olivi's violated grave, Clement V's summons, the audiences before John XXII in 1317 ('Nolumus, nolumus'; 'ask them why they drove me out'; 'you wear five tunics'), the four burned at Marseille, Bonagratia interrogating Bernard Délicieux, the question of 1321 and Clareno's verdict on the order that now defended poverty, Ubertino made a monk, and Francis's habit in the form of a cross.

units.orig: Huius malignitatis livore et corrumpenti ac devoranti rubigine infecti et maculati fuerunt communiter omnes sexte tribulationis auctores et promotores et presertim illi, qui procuraverunt tempore domini Bonifacii carcerationem fratrum plurimorum sanctorum provincie Provincie post depositionem ministri generalis et animose dampnaverunt doctrinam viri sancti Petri Johannis et ossibus et reliquiis eius in tenebris violato sepulcro ipsius ut tenebrarum ministri occultam iniuriam intulerunt.
units.en: With the envy of this malignity, and with its corrupting and devouring rust, all the authors and promoters of the sixth tribulation were commonly infected and stained, and above all those who, in the time of the lord Boniface, after the deposition of the minister general, procured the imprisonment of very many holy brothers of the province of Provence, and passionately condemned the teaching of the holy man Peter John, and, violating his tomb in the dark, did hidden injury to his bones and relics, like ministers of darkness.
units.note: Clareno counts the history of the order as seven tribulations, persecutions of the true followers of Francis by their own brothers; the sixth runs from the deposition of the Spiritual-minded general Raymond Geoffroi (1295) to John XXII. The page before is a treatise on envy as the root of all persecution. The holy man is Peter John Olivi (d. 1298), whose tomb at Narbonne the Beguins venerated (Practica [2]).

units.titel: A physician speaks to a king
units.orig: Tunc siluerunt, latuerunt et absentaverunt se ex eis plurimi ruinam gladii persequencium non ferrentes, fueruntque suppressura (sub pressura) persequencium, donec deus per hominem amatorem veritatis magistrum Reinaldum de Villa Nova medicum, qui locutus fuit cum Carulo rege Cecilie et induxit eum ad scribendum litteras efficaces generali ministro pro fratribus illis, qui iniustas tribulationes sustinebant in provincia Provincie. In quibus litteris notificabat ei, quod si debitum festinumque remedium non apponeret eorum iniuste tribulacioni, quod hoc fieri per summum pontificem firmiter procuraret. Qui magister predictus celans pro reformatione evangelici status secrete dominum Clementem summum pontificem induxit ad citandum corum eo fr. Reymundum Gaufridi et fr. Guidonem de Mirabice et fr. Ubertinum de Casali et fr. Bartholomeum Siccardi et reliquos eorum socios viros vite sancte et sciencie preclare, eciam testimonio emulorum; et precipere eis per obedientiam districte, offerre ei in scriptis quecunque scirent et cognoscerent in statu ordinis eorum fieri, que correctione et reformatione indigerent.
units.en: Then very many of them fell silent, hid and took themselves away, not bearing the ruin of the persecutors' sword, and they were under the pressure of the persecutors, until God, through a man who loved the truth, Master Arnau de Vilanova, a physician, who spoke with Charles, king of Sicily, and moved him to write effective letters to the minister general for those brothers who were suffering unjust tribulations in the province of Provence. In these letters he let him know that if he did not apply a due and speedy remedy to their unjust tribulation, he would firmly see to it that this was done by the supreme pontiff. And the said master, zealous for the reform of the gospel state, secretly moved the lord Clement, the supreme pontiff, to summon before him Brother Raymond Geoffroi, Brother Guy of Mirepoix, Brother Ubertino of Casale, Brother Bartholomew Sicardi and the rest of their companions, men of holy life and outstanding learning, even by the testimony of their rivals; and to order them strictly under obedience to set before him in writing whatever they knew and recognized to be done in the state of their order that needed correction and reform.
units.note: Arnau de Vilanova (d. 1311), physician to kings and popes and himself a writer on the Apocalypse; Charles II of Anjou, king of Naples, who still called himself king of Sicily. Clement V's summons (1309–1310) opened the hearings that led to the Council of Vienne and to Exivi de paradiso (Exivi [2]). The sentence breaks off in the manuscript: the Italian version reads 'until God came to help through that man'.

units.orig: Deo autem disponente per illustrem catholicum et sapientem virum dominum Philippum regem Francie cardinalium collegium tunc in tres partes enormiter, spiritu maligno impugnante, divisum, Lugdunum deductum conclave de consensu parcium ad elleccionem summi pontificis faciendum intrare persuasum est; ubi non post multos dies in dominum Jacobum de Caturcho cardinalem omnes concordaverunt, et provisum est ecclesie a deo in die s. Donati et vocatus est Johannes, quasi a deo datus et missus. Qui omnium, que acta fuerunt inter fratres tempore diuturno plene erat ex hiis, que viderat et audierat, informatus et divisionem illam habebat in displicenciam et moleste portabat. Ad quem cum fratres minores accessissent, mandavit provinciali ministro, fratribus illis precipere ex parte sua, quod loca dimitterent et conformes aliis fratribus in habitu et vita esse deberent et quod ad illa loca accederent ad morandum, que minister provincialis eis duceret adsignanda, eidem suppliciter obedientes in omnibus, que mandaret. Illi vero determinaverunt penitus ad summum pontificem velle accedere et puram regule observanciam instanter ab ipso postulare et sue ad ipsum appellacionis raciones et causas coram ponere et eius pocius quam fratrum, qui eos ad mortem oderant, subire sentenciam.
units.en: By God's disposition, then, through the illustrious, catholic and wise man, the lord Philip, king of France, the college of cardinals, which the evil spirit had then divided grievously into three parties, was brought to Lyon and persuaded, with the consent of the parties, to enter conclave to elect the supreme pontiff; where, not many days later, they all agreed on the lord James of Cahors, cardinal, and the Church was provided for by God on the day of Saint Donatus, and he was called John, as if given and sent by God. He was fully informed of everything that had happened among the brothers over a long time, from what he had seen and heard, and he disliked that division and bore it ill. When the Friars Minor came to him, he ordered the provincial minister to command those brothers, on his behalf, to leave their houses, to conform to the other brothers in habit and life, and to go to live in the houses the provincial minister thought fit to assign them, obeying him humbly in everything he commanded. But they resolved absolutely to go to the supreme pontiff, to ask him urgently for the pure observance of the rule, to set before him the reasons and causes of their appeal to him, and to submit to his sentence rather than that of the brothers, who hated them to the death.
units.note: 7 August 1316, the feast of Saint Donatus, at Lyon; Philip is Philip V, then regent of France. 'Johannes', which Clareno glosses as 'given by God', was a pope he had welcomed. 'Those brothers' are the Spirituals who had taken over the convents of Narbonne and Béziers.

units.orig: Et cum fr. Ubertinus confutasset omnia, que fratres proposuerant et ostendisset esse falsa et ex malicia et invidia procedere que dicebant, interrogavit summus pontifex fr. Ubertinum, an ipse adhereret fratribus de Narbona et de Biterris, et an ipse vellet fr. Petri Johannis doctrinam defendere; Ubertinus respondit: 'Pater sancte, ego in hiis, que olim feci, obedienciam vestri predecessoris implevi et a me ipso in hiis penitus nichil feci; unde si vestre paternitati placet, mihi precipere quod ego pro fratribus de Narbona et sociis vel pro doctrina fr. Petri nunc questionem assumam, ecce paratus sum vestre voluntati in omnibus obedire'. Cui summus pontifex respondit: 'Nolumus, nolumus, quod intromittatis vos'.
units.en: And when Brother Ubertino had refuted everything the brothers had put forward, and shown that what they said was false and came from malice and envy, the supreme pontiff asked Brother Ubertino whether he adhered to the brothers of Narbonne and Béziers, and whether he wished to defend the teaching of Brother Peter John. Ubertino answered: 'Holy father, in what I once did I fulfilled the obedience of your predecessor, and did nothing at all of myself; so, if it please your paternity to command me to take up the question now for the brothers of Narbonne and their companions, or for the teaching of Brother Peter, see, I am ready to obey your will in everything.' The supreme pontiff answered him: 'We do not wish it, we do not wish it, that you should meddle.'
units.note: Ubertino of Casale (1259–c. 1329), the leader of the Spirituals at Vienne and author of the Arbor vitae. The friars of the Community had accused him, the brothers of Tuscany, the convents of Narbonne and Béziers, the 'Beguins' and Angelo himself. The pope keeps the most formidable defender of the Spirituals out of the case.

units.orig: Cum vero venisset fr. Angelus coram eo, interrogavit eum, an ipse esset frater minor; cui ille respondit, quod sic. Et dixit ad eum summus pontifex: 'Quare recessisti ab eis'? Respondit fr. Angelus: 'Pater sancte ego non recessi ab eis; sed interrogate eos, quare repulerunt me'. Et siluit summus pontifex; et iterum dixit ei: 'Precipio tibi quod dicas michi, si tu unquam confessiones audisti'. Qui respondit: 'Pater sancte non sum sacerdos; et una de racionibus, quare nolui esse sacerdos est, quia nolebam audire confessiones; unde ego nullius confessionem audivi'. Et post aliquas alias interrogaciones precepit fratribus, quod legerent litteras domini pape Bonifacii et domini patriarche Constantinopolitani, quibus lectis dixit summus pontifex fratri Angelo: 'Frater Angele tu es excommunicatus'. Respondit fr. Angelus: 'Pater sancte nec excommunicatus nec excommunicabilis, cum semper obediverim tam domino Bonifacio quam patriarche et ceteris prelatis ecclesie'. Et cum inciperet dicere et ostendere, quomodo ille lictere maliciose et cum mendaciis fuerant impetrate et reservate, et quomodo fratres contra illas licteras scienter venerant et nullam de ipsis conscienciam habuerant, sed operibus et sermone ipsas iniquas et inique impetratas confessi fuerant, non potuit summus pontifex eum audire, sed impedivit eum, ne compleret que dicere ceperat. Tunc fr. Angelus dixit: 'Pater sancte, vos audistis mendacia fratrum et veritatem, quam vobis dico, non sustinetis audire'. Erat autem hora quasi sexta.
units.en: When Brother Angelo came before him, he asked him whether he was a Friar Minor; he answered that he was. And the supreme pontiff said to him: 'Why did you leave them?' Brother Angelo answered: 'Holy father, I did not leave them; ask them why they drove me out.' And the supreme pontiff was silent; and again he said to him: 'I command you to tell me whether you have ever heard confessions.' He answered: 'Holy father, I am not a priest; and one of the reasons why I did not wish to be a priest is that I did not wish to hear confessions; so I have heard no one's confession.' And after some other questions he ordered the brothers to read the letters of the lord Pope Boniface and of the lord patriarch of Constantinople; when they had been read, the supreme pontiff said to Brother Angelo: 'Brother Angelo, you are excommunicated.' Brother Angelo answered: 'Holy father, neither excommunicated nor excommunicable, since I have always obeyed both the lord Boniface and the patriarch and the other prelates of the Church.' And when he began to say and show how those letters had been obtained and kept back with malice and lies, and how the brothers had knowingly acted against those letters and had no conscience about them, but had confessed by deed and word that they were unjust and unjustly obtained, the supreme pontiff could not listen to him, but stopped him from finishing what he had begun to say. Then Brother Angelo said: 'Holy father, you have heard the lies of the brothers, and the truth that I tell you, you cannot bear to hear.' It was about the sixth hour.
units.note: Brother Angelo is the author himself, Angelo Clareno (c. 1250–1337), telling his own hearing in the third person. He had been sent to Armenia and then led a group of Spirituals in Greece and Italy under the protection of Celestine V; Boniface VIII's letters against them are the ones read out. Afterwards the pope held him in custody, then allowed him to take the habit of the Celestine hermits: he promised to live 'in the highest poverty of Christ'.

units.orig: Circa festum vero pentecostes venerunt sexaginta quatuor fratres ad summum pontificem de conventu Narbone et Biterris et non declinaverunt ad loca fratrum, sed intrantes in Avinionem ad summi pontificis palacium accesserunt et pre foribus palacii illa nocte steterunt nec recesserunt, donec summus pontifex audienciam eis dedit. Proposuit autem unus ex eis nomine fr. Berardus Deliciosi, vir magne modestie et preclare sciencie et diserte eloquencie, coram summo pontifice et cardinalium collegio tam prudenter et circumspecte et efficaciter, quod ad ea, que dicebat et postulabat, nulla ab adversariis instancia racionabiliter poterat dari. [...] Nam ipse pro se et pro fratribus aliis nichil proponebat nec postulabat nisi id, quod eis iuste negari non poterat, observanciam videlicet fidelem et puram promisse regule et remociones impugnancium observanciam necessariam ad salutem. Cum autem satisfacere vellet predictus frater et calumpnias suas personales confutare et reducere eos ad causam, pro qua coram summo pontifice stabat, fratres adversarii instabant proponentes alia contra eum, donec papa conversus ad fr. Berardum dixit: 'Et nos propter multa mala, que de te audivimus, detinemus te'.
units.en: Around the feast of Pentecost sixty-four brothers of the convents of Narbonne and Béziers came to the supreme pontiff, and did not turn aside to the houses of the brothers, but entered Avignon and went to the supreme pontiff's palace, and stood that night before the doors of the palace and did not go away until the supreme pontiff gave them a hearing. One of them, named Brother Bernard Délicieux, a man of great modesty, outstanding learning and ready eloquence, spoke before the supreme pontiff and the college of cardinals so prudently, circumspectly and effectively that no reasonable objection could be made by his adversaries to what he said and asked. [...] For he proposed and asked nothing, for himself or for the other brothers, except what could not justly be denied them: the faithful and pure observance of the rule they had promised, and the removal of those who attacked the observance necessary to salvation. But when the said brother wished to answer, to refute the personal slanders against him and bring them back to the cause for which he stood before the supreme pontiff, the adversary brothers pressed on, putting forward other charges against him, until the pope turned to Brother Bernard and said: 'And we, for the many evils we have heard of you, hold you in custody.'
units.note: Pentecost 1317 (the Italian version agrees; one manuscript reads Easter). Bernard Délicieux had led the resistance of Carcassonne to the Dominican inquisition twenty years earlier; the cut gives the friars' reply that he had 'presumed to hinder the office of the inquisition'. He was tried in 1319 and died in prison. The two men heard next, Francesco Sanchez and Guillaume de Saint-Amans, were silenced the same way.

units.orig: Summus vero pontifex, licet eum inter alios magis familiarem habuisset, dixit ei: 'Frater Gaufride non modicum amiramur, quod regule artam postulas observanciam et tu quinque tunicas portas'. Respondit ei fr. Gaufridus: 'Pater sancte vos in hoc decipimini, quia non est verum, quod ego V tunicas portem, salva vestra reverencia'. Et dixit ei summus pontifex: 'Ergo mentimur nos'. Dixit ei fr. Gaufridus: 'Pater sancte ego non dixi neque dicerem, quod vos mentimini, sed dixi et dico, quod non est verum, quod ego V tunicas portem'. Et dixit ei summus pontifex: 'Nos detinemus te et sciemus, si verum est quod tu V tunicas portes'. Videntes vero alii, quod audiencia non daretur eis clamaverunt: 'Pater sancte iusticia, iusticia'.
units.en: But the supreme pontiff, although he had held him more familiar than the others, said to him: 'Brother Geoffroy, we are not a little surprised that you ask for the strict observance of the rule and you wear five tunics.' Brother Geoffroy answered him: 'Holy father, you are deceived in this, for it is not true that I wear five tunics, saving your reverence.' And the supreme pontiff said to him: 'So we are lying.' Brother Geoffroy said to him: 'Holy father, I did not say and would not say that you are lying, but I said and say that it is not true that I wear five tunics.' And the supreme pontiff said to him: 'We hold you in custody, and we shall find out whether it is true that you wear five tunics.' Seeing that they were not given a hearing, the others cried out: 'Holy father, justice, justice.'
units.note: Geoffroy, a noble and a sick man, the one the friars 'could not accuse or defame' as they had the others. The rule allowed one tunic with a hood and, for those who wished, another without; the pope's jibe turns the Spirituals' own measure against them. Short and patched habits were the other half of Quorundam exigit (Decr. Exigit [2]).

units.titel: Twenty-five to the inquisitor, four to the fire
units.orig: Et mandavit eis omnibus summus pontifex, quod redirent ad locum fratrum, et fratribus, quod custodirent eos, donec maturius deliberaret, quid de ipsis esset agendum. Camerarius vero domini pape suscepit in sua custodia fratres Berardum de Liciosi et fr. Gaufridum et Gulhelmum de s. Amancio; fr. Franciscum Sanccii posuerunt fratres in quodam carcere iuxta latrinas. Et post paucos dies carceraverunt fr. Gulhelmum Girardi et fr. Philippum; et facta de ipsis inquisicione iuxta domini pape mandatum, exceptis XXV fratribus, omnes consenserunt fratrum consiliis et voluntatibus. Et fratres imposuerunt eis penitencias secundum rigorem iusticie ordinis; illos autem XXV tradiderunt in manibus inquisitoris, ex quibus quatuor combusti sunt pro eo, quod asserebant regulam s. Francisci esse idem, quod ewangelium Christi; quod solempniter promissum cadit in preceptum, eo quod tale votum habet vim precepti, specialiter in hiis, que regula preceptorie vel inhibitorie mandat, et talia, dicebant, non cadunt sub dispensacione alicuius. Asserebant eciam, quod summus pontifex non potuerat fratribus minoribus, qui promiserunt Christi ewangelium, concedere celaria, granaria et olearia; et quod papa peccaverat concedendo et ipsi recipiendo. Et quia ab hac assercione non potuerunt per aliquem revocari, ideo sentenciam ignis acceperunt.
units.en: And the supreme pontiff ordered them all to return to the brothers' house, and the brothers to keep them in custody until he had deliberated more fully what should be done with them. The lord pope's chamberlain took into his custody Brothers Bernard Délicieux, Geoffroy and Guillaume de Saint-Amans; Brother Francesco Sanchez the brothers put in a prison next to the latrines. And after a few days they imprisoned Brother Guillaume Girard and Brother Philip; and when an inquiry had been made into them by the lord pope's order, all except twenty-five consented to the counsels and will of the brothers. And the brothers imposed penances on them according to the rigour of the order's justice; but those twenty-five they handed over into the hands of the inquisitor, and of them four were burned because they asserted that the rule of Saint Francis is the same as the Gospel of Christ; that what is solemnly promised falls under precept, because such a vow has the force of a precept, especially in the things the rule commands or forbids; and such things, they said, fall under no one's dispensation. They asserted also that the supreme pontiff could not grant cellars, granaries and oil stores to the Friars Minor, who had promised the Gospel of Christ, and that the pope had sinned in granting it and they in receiving it. And because no one could make them withdraw from this assertion, they received the sentence of fire.
units.note: Marseille, 7 May 1318; the inquisitor was the Franciscan Michel Le Moine. The Beguins of Languedoc venerated the four as martyrs (Practica [9]), and Pierre Dominici was burned at Toulouse partly for saying so (Sent. Dominici [3]). A fifth, who recanted late, was walled up for life.

units.orig: Tenebatur autem predictus fr. Berardus Deliciosi in cippo et vinculis ferreis et sustentabatur pane angustie et aqua tribulacionis. Set totum, quod paciebatur a persequentibus eum, quasi nichil esse penitus sibi videbatur. Et adinvenciones eorum et studia convertebant, si quomodo de ore ipsius verbum possent aliquod capere vel extorquere, per quod occasionem haberent, contra eum quasi contra hereticum procedendi. Accedebat ad eum princeps litigiorum fr. Bonagracia armatus cautelis et consultacionibus suorum quondam in seculo sociorum, et beatitudinis sue gloriam singularem optinere se tunc veraciter credidisset, si potuisset versutis et dolosis inquisicionibus eum quomodolibet supplantare. Sed vir dei manswetudine christiana et sapiencia plenus ei et suis coadiutoribus taliter respondebat, quod per eum proposita ostendebat non fuisse tantum catholica, sed necessaria ad salutem et tam solida et fidelia, quod non possent negari a quoquam vel impugnari absque negacione et impugnacione fidei christiane.
units.en: The said Brother Bernard Délicieux was held in the stocks and in iron chains, and was fed on the bread of affliction and the water of tribulation. But everything he suffered from his persecutors seemed to him as nothing at all. And they turned their inventions and efforts to seeing whether they could somehow catch or extort some word from his mouth that would give them occasion to proceed against him as against a heretic. To him came the prince of litigation, Brother Bonagratia, armed with the tricks and counsels of his former companions in the world, and he would truly have believed he had won the singular glory of his blessedness if he could somehow have tripped him up with his cunning and deceitful questioning. But the man of God, full of Christian gentleness and wisdom, answered him and his helpers in such a way that he showed what he had put forward to be not only catholic but necessary to salvation, and so solid and faithful that no one could deny or attack it without denying and attacking the Christian faith.
units.note: Bonagratia of Bergamo, a lawyer before he became a friar ('his former companions in the world'), was in 1317 the Community's prosecutor against the Spirituals. Five years later he was the order's procurator who appealed against Ad conditorem and was imprisoned for it (Chron. Appeal [1]), and in 1328 he fled from Avignon with Michael and Ockham (Chron. Flight [1]). Clareno wrote knowing both halves of the story.

units.titel: The seventh tribulation, and the same spirit
units.orig: (Hic incipere potest tribulatio septima). Post hec questio orta est, ut dicitur, Narbone inter predicatores et minores, an Christus et apostoli proprium habuerint in communi. Quam questionem sanctus dei homo Petrus Johannes late et diffuse tractavit et diffinivit. Et dei nutu pro veritate steterunt fratres minores, quam ille magnus eorum hereticus et condam anathema, innumeris racionibus et sanctorum auctoritatibus realissimis munitam clarissime probavit. Pro qua veritate firmiter et perseveranter stare verbo et opere, corde puro et consciencia bona et fide non ficta usque in finem det eis Christus Jhesus, qui patri eorum apparuit et seraphyce et cruciformis caritatis sue signaculis insignivit eum [...]. Cum enim secundum veritatem nichil aliud dyabolus tantum per se et suos satellites et sequaces radicare conatus fuerit de religione fundata per Franciscum quantum altissime paupertatis nuditatem [...]; valde formidandum est, ne eodem spiritu agantur ad pugnandum et defendendum paupertatis ewangelice nuditatem, quo agebantur ad resistendum fundatori et ad persequendum amantes observare fideliter et sincere promisse paupertatis certam securitatem et nudissimam puritatem. [...] Quid enim aliud impugnaverunt et persecuti sunt fratres in suis patribus et fratribus Cesario, Berardo, Symone, Matheo, Johanne de Parma et Petro, Petro Johanne, Poncio Botugati, Raymundo Gaufridi et Ubertino nisi fidem et confessionem et operacionem illius ewangelice paupertatis, pro qua modo cum suis emulis, ne nomen sine re perdant ewangelici status, unanimiter et cordialiter certant.
units.en: (Here the seventh tribulation may begin.) After this a question arose, it is said, at Narbonne between the Preachers and the Minors, whether Christ and the apostles had property in common. This question the holy man of God, Peter John, had treated and settled at length and in detail. And by God's will the Friars Minor stood for the truth which that great 'heretic' of theirs, that 'former anathema', had proved most clearly, fortified with countless reasons and the most solid authorities of the saints. May Christ Jesus grant them to stand for that truth firmly and perseveringly, in word and deed, with a pure heart, a good conscience and unfeigned faith, to the end; he who appeared to their father and marked him with the seals of his seraphic and cross-shaped love [...]. For since in truth the devil, by himself and his henchmen and followers, has tried to root out nothing from the religion founded by Francis so much as the nakedness of the highest poverty [...], it is greatly to be feared that they are driven to fight for and defend the nakedness of gospel poverty by the same spirit by which they were driven to resist the founder and to persecute those who loved to keep faithfully and sincerely the sure security and the most naked purity of the poverty they had promised. [...] For what else did the brothers attack and persecute in their fathers and brothers Caesar, Bernard, Simon, Matthew, John of Parma and Peter, Peter John, Pons Botugati, Raymond Geoffroi and Ubertino, but the faith, confession and practice of that gospel poverty for which they now fight, with one mind and heart, against their rivals, lest they lose the name of the gospel state without the thing?
units.note: The question of 1321 at Narbonne, where a Dominican inquisitor judged a Beguin's claim that Christ had nothing, even in common, and a Franciscan lector protested; the pope opened the question in March 1322 (Decr. Nonnunquam [3]) and the order answered at Perugia (Chron. Perugia [2]). Clareno's verdict on Michael's party is the thesis of this site from the other side: the Community now defended in Olivi's words the poverty it had persecuted in Olivi's followers, and did so to keep 'the name without the thing'.

units.orig: Timentes enim, ne in futurum loqueretur contra eos fr. Ubertinus, cum exclusus esset ex mandato summi pontificis ab eorum negocio et ipse sibi attenderet post diffinicionem per summum pontificem datam et de eorum litigiis non curaret, tanta cum indignacione ferebantur adversus eum, ut omne quod de aliis fecerant, putarent esse nichil, quandiu ille superesset et viveret super terram. Infestabant igitur cotidie summum pontificem, et peticionibus et precibus importunis incessanter fatigabant eum, postulantes fr. Ubertinum sibi redi, cum esset mora sua in curia ordini verecundia intollerabilis et maximum detrimentum. Vocabat summus pontifex fr. Ubertinum ad instanciam fratrum et rogabat eum, quod pro aliquibus diebus deberet cum fratribus moram trahere, quia cito, postquam fratribus satisfecisset de mora, ei secundum sui status congruenciam provideret. Cui fr. Ubertinus respondebat: Post moram meam unius diei cum ipsis non indigebo nec vestra nec cuiusquam alterius provisione in hac vita. [...] propter quod unum de duobus se facturum de fr. Ubertino, ab eorum importunitate levare se volens, eis deliberasse se dicit: Vel enim revertetur ad vos, inquid, vel alterius religionis statum et habitum sumet. Quod cum innotuisset fr. Ubertino, de secundo consensit, sperans se summum pontificem posse vel difficultate peticionum vel racionum modesta persuasione posse immutare. Sed quia neutrum potuit, difficultate peticionum eum quantum valuit retardavit. Summus vero pontifex volens de secundo, quia faciem iusticie videbatur habere, fratribus satisfacere, omnia que ab ipso postulavit sub sue bulle munimine semel et secundo sigillata concessit.
units.en: For fearing that Brother Ubertino might speak against them in future, although he had been excluded from their business by the supreme pontiff's order and kept to himself after the pope had given his decision and did not concern himself with their quarrels, they were carried against him with such indignation that they thought everything they had done to the others was nothing as long as he survived and lived upon the earth. So they harassed the supreme pontiff daily and wearied him incessantly with petitions and importunate prayers, demanding that Brother Ubertino be given back to them, since his staying at the curia was an intolerable shame and the greatest harm to the order. At the brothers' request the supreme pontiff called Brother Ubertino and asked him to stay with the brothers for a few days, because as soon as he had satisfied the brothers by that stay he would soon provide for him according to what befitted his state. Brother Ubertino answered him: 'After staying one day with them I shall need neither your provision nor anyone else's in this life.' [...] So, wishing to be relieved of their importunity, the pope said he had decided to do one of two things with Brother Ubertino: 'Either he will return to you,' he said, 'or he will take the state and habit of another religious order.' When Brother Ubertino learned this, he consented to the second, hoping he might change the supreme pontiff's mind either by the difficulty of his requests or by the modest persuasion of reasons. But since he could do neither, he delayed him as much as he could by the difficulty of his requests. And the supreme pontiff, wishing to satisfy the brothers with the second course, because it seemed to have the face of justice, granted everything he asked, sealed under his bull once and a second time.
units.note: 'After one day with them I shall need no one's provision in this life': he expected to be killed. The papal letter of 1 October 1317 allowed Ubertino to pass to the Benedictines of Gembloux (Ehrle's note). He did not stay a monk in any quiet sense: in 1325 the pope ordered his arrest, and in 1328 he is said to have preached for Louis in Rome.

units.titel: The habit in the form of a cross
units.orig: Voluit autem b. Franciscus a Christo doctus et habitum suum exteriorem cruciformem ad litteram esse. Unde mensuram sui habitus, latitudinem, longitudinem, qualitatem quoad vilitatem et colorem docuit verbo et exemplo firmavit, testibus fr. Leone de Assisio, fr. Berardo Quintavalle, Egidio de Assisio et Masseo Marignani et aliis sociis suis, qui se ab eo formam habitus accepisse dicebant et opere testabantur. Quo ad materiam docuit, quod esset de panno vili et coloris cinericii vel pallidi, corporis Christi mortificacionem representantis; et talis grossiciei, quod corpus foveret et posset fratri sano una tunica sufficere intus et foris repeciata; tante longitudinis, quod succincta absque collacione super cingulum terram non attingeret. Longitudo manicarum usque ad extremitates digitorum, ita quod manus operiret et longitudinem manuum non excederet; latitudo earum esset tanta, quod manus libere exire posset et intrare. Capucium quadrum et tante longitudinis, quod faciem operiret, ita quod habitus crucis formam representaret et omnis mundane glorie et ornatus contemptum sua vilitate predicaret et fratrem minorem mundo crucifixum et mortuum ostenderet, et esset nuditatis operimentum et necessitatis amatorum paupertatis fomentum, et professorum humilitatis signum, et portacionis improperii crucis Christi verum indicium.
units.en: Blessed Francis, taught by Christ, wished his outward habit to be literally in the form of a cross. So he taught by word and confirmed by example the measure of his habit, its width, its length, its quality as to cheapness, and its colour, as Brother Leo of Assisi, Brother Bernard of Quintavalle, Giles of Assisi, Masseo of Marignano and his other companions testified, who said they had received the form of the habit from him and showed it in practice. As to the material, he taught that it should be of cheap cloth, of an ashen or pale colour, representing the mortification of Christ's body; and so coarse that it would keep the body warm, and one tunic, patched inside and out, could suffice for a healthy brother; so long that, girded, without being drawn up over the cord, it would not touch the ground. The sleeves should reach to the tips of the fingers, so as to cover the hands and not be longer than the hands; and wide enough for the hand to go in and out freely. The hood square and long enough to cover the face, so that the habit would show the form of a cross, preach by its cheapness contempt for all worldly glory and adornment, and show the Friar Minor crucified and dead to the world; and it would be a covering for nakedness, a comfort in the necessity of lovers of poverty, a sign of the professors of humility, and a true mark of bearing the reproach of Christ's cross.
units.note: The Spirituals' short, narrow and patched habits were what John XXII ordered them to put off in 1317 (Decr. Exigit [2]); here the habit is measured as Francis's first companions are said to have measured it, down to the length of the sleeves. 'Berardo Quintavalle' is as printed, for Bernard of Quintavalle, the first companion (Par. XI [7]).
